newsitem.title: UK: Battle lines drawn for British Co-op showdown.
newsitem.headline: Battle lines drawn for British Co-op showdown.

text.p: The battle for Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) will intensify this week as the two sides square up in the High Court amid an increasingly bitter contest.
A High Court process begins on Tuesday to decide what information the bidder, 31-year-old entreprenuer Andrew Regan, may use in a hostile bid he plans for the supermarkets-to-funeral parlour mammoth.

In a separate move, CWS chief Graham Melmoth stepped up the pressure with a warning to Regan that the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) would be called in if Regan failed to answer certain questions CWS had over payments it said Regan had made.
"Tomorrow's court case is the main focus, they will all have to be there," one source told Reuters.

CWS faxed Regan a letter on Monday demanding he answers questions concerning payments of over two million pounds it said Regan had made for a company called Trellis, which it linked to his 1994 purchase of CWS's food manufacturing arm.

Regan is weighing a 1.0-to-1.50 billion pound ($1.6 to 2.4 billion) bid for CWS, which has a multi-billion pound turnover from businesses ranging from supermarkets to insurance and the Co-operative Bank.
But the group has struggled to turn its massive revenues into profit.
Last week it announced a 10 million pound ($16.3 million) fall in pre-tax profits to 54.1 million pounds for the year to January 11 and Regan is not alone is studying CWS assets.
On Sunday the Allied Irish Banks Plc said it was interested in buying the profitable Co-op Bank but denied a deal was already in place.
Retailer J. Sainsbury Plc declined to comment on "speculation" that it might buy some of the the Co-op's retail outlets.

Galileo Group, a special bidding vehicle part-owned by Regan's Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica, said last Friday it would propose converting the CWS to a limited company in order to make an offer for the whole group.

But Galileo's immediate ambitions were thwarted after CWS obtained a court order preventing Galileo, Lanica, Regan, his associate David Lyons or a suspended senior CWS manager, from using any confidential information they may have on the group.

Under the terms of the court order they must also provide sworn affidavits by 1500 GMT on Tuesday detailing what information they have received. The court will then consider the case and has scheduled a hearing for Friday morning.
The court move followed the suspension last Thursday of two senior CWS executives, Allan Green and David Chambers, for an alleged breach of trust.

Galileo acknowledged the court action had stymied its plans "for the time being". A spokesman for Regan said Galileo's overriding objective was to put its proposals to CWS members and it would be up to them to decide whether or not to accept them.

A source close to the bid, which is backed by City institutions including Jupiter Asset Management Ltd, Schroders Investment Management (UK) Ltd and stockbrokers Killick & Co, said a takeover attempt could be relauched by the end of the week. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
